title: DDRop Attack Breaks Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP With $159 DDR5 Device
content_md: Security researchers have disclosed DDRop, a low-cost hardware attack that can undermine confidential-computing protections in Intel TDX, Intel Scalable SGX, and AMD SEV-SNP systems. The attack uses a custom DDR5 memory interposer costing about $159 in parts and requires privileged software access plus brief physical access to the target server. Trusted Execution Environments, or TEEs, are designed to protect sensitive workloads from cloud providers, hypervisors, and other highly privileged software. Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP encrypt virtual-machine memory, making it difficult for a malicious host administrator to directly read protected data. DDRop Breaches Intel AMD TEEs However, the researchers found that these platforms lack cryptographic freshness protection. In simple terms, the processor can verify that encrypted memory data appears valid, but it may not detect that the data is old. This creates an opening for a physical attacker to force a protected workload to use stale memory contents. DDRop places a small device between a server CPU and a DDR5 Registered DIMM. The device interferes with DDR5 memory commands at normal operating speeds. It deliberately causes parity errors on the command bus and disconnects the alert signal that would normally notify the CPU of the error.
